title: The Price of a Cup

pages.text:
*The Bearer's Almanac, Entry 10: When water has a price, someone has put a gate where there was none.*

The town of Shitou clung to the cliff face like a barnacle that had decided to grow legs. It was not a place you entered so much as a place you climbed into, tier by tier, along a zigzagging path cut into the living rock. The air smelled of dried herbs and hot stone, and the silence was different here, thinner, as if the mountain was holding its breath.

At the center of the lowest tier stood the fountain. It was a large, square basin of grey granite, carved with lotus flowers that had long since lost their meaning in the dry season. The basin was empty. Not low, not trickling, but completely, stubbornly empty. A single pigeon stood on the dry lip, tilting its head with the profound irritation of a landlord whose tenant has stopped paying rent.

Wen walked past it with her boots clicking against the flagstones, trying to ignore the sound. The clicking was too loud, too deliberate, and it drew eyes from the shadows of the shopfronts. People watched her with a mixture of curiosity and suspicion, the way one watches a stray dog that has wandered into a tidy kitchen. She kept her chin up and her hands tucked into the sleeves of her pale linen tunic, though her fingers were itching to touch the dust on the ground, to feel if there was any moisture left in the roots of the mountain.

Then she saw the stall.

It was a modest affair, a wooden counter set against a low wall, but the goods on it were arranged with a fastidious precision that made Wen’s stomach turn. Row upon row of sealed clay jars, each one stamped with a round gate seal, sat in neat lines. The clay was dark, almost black, and the water inside was visible through the translucent glass of the lids, clear and cold and impossible.

A sign hung above the jars, painted in brushstrokes so fine they looked like veins. *Clean water. By the cup. Ten times the price of rice.*

Wen stopped. She looked at the jars, then at the dry fountain, and felt a cold knot tighten in her chest. This was not scarcity. This was a business model.
pages.image: A narrow cliffside town tiered along grey rock, an empty square granite fountain basin, a wooden stall with rows of dark clay jars stamped with round seals, Wen in a pale tunic and blue ponytail standing small before the stall, dry dusty light.

pages.text:
Shen Yu stood at the counter, his brass-rimmed glasses sliding down his nose as he leaned in to inspect the jars rather than simply buying one. He picked up a vessel, turned it over in his hands, and traced the seal with an ink-stained finger.

"Shen Yu," Wen said, keeping her voice low. "What is that?"

He did not look up. "A Cistern seal," he murmured. "I have seen it on the tax rolls in the valley below. It is not local. It is not from the river."

Master Gao, who had been standing behind them with his arms crossed and a smile of practiced ease on his face, stepped forward. "A common merchant mark," he said, his voice smooth as oiled silk. "Many traders use the same symbol. It is a sign of quality, nothing more. Do not read too much into a stamp on a jar."

Shen Yu looked up, his eyes sharp behind the lenses. "The seal is pressed into the clay before it is fired," he said. "The clay is from the upper basin. I know the texture. It is not from this cliff. It is from the White Basin, or beyond."

Gao’s smile did not waver, but his eyes flickered to the jars, then to Shen Yu, then to Wen. "You are a surveyor, boy," he said. "You measure lines. You do not measure loyalty. Let the merchant sell his water. We have our own gourd."

Wen looked at Gao. He was tall, his green robe immaculate, his jade hairpin catching the light. He looked like a man who had never had to worry about where his next cup of water would come from. She looked at Shen Yu, whose face had gone paler still. She looked at the jars, and the cold knot in her chest tightened again.

She wanted to believe Gao. She wanted to believe that this was just a coincidence, a strange and cruel coincidence. But the seal on the jar looked back at her, round and closed, and she had the distinct, uncomfortable feeling of a gate sliding shut.
pages.image: Shen Yu in a brown vest and glasses examining a dark clay jar with a round seal, Master Gao in a green robe and jade hairpin standing behind with a polite smile, Wen in a pale tunic watching them, a wooden counter and jars in the foreground, soft dusty light.

pages.text:
The merchant was a small, sharp-eyed woman who barely looked at them. She did not ask who they were. She did not offer a discount. She simply stood behind her counter, her hands folded on the wood, and waited.

It was her daughter who spoke. She was young, perhaps thirteen, with a smudge of clay on her cheek and a look of weary defiance in her dark eyes. She did not step forward, but her voice carried easily in the quiet street.

"The water comes by night," she said. "Covered carts. They do not stop here. They go on to the next tier. The next town. Always north."

Wen felt a chill that had nothing to do with the temperature. "North," she repeated. "Up the river?"

"The carts are heavy," the girl said. "They do not travel far in the day. The drivers do not sleep. They change horses at the upper road. The dust is still wet when the sun comes up. You can follow the track."

Shen Yu was already moving, his surveyor’s staff tapping against the flagstones. "A wet track," he murmured. "If the carts pass at night, the dust will hold the moisture until morning. It will look different from the dry dust. It will be darker. Denser."

Gao laughed, a soft, amused sound. "You are a clever boy, Shen Yu. But we are travelers, not spies. We have a road to walk and a river to find. Let us not get lost in the mud of this town."

Wen looked at the girl. Her eyes were hard, but there was a fear behind them, a thin, brittle fear that made Wen’s chest ache. This was not just about water. This was about control. Someone was moving water up the river, sealing it in jars, and selling it back to the people who had been living with the river for generations. And they were doing it in the dark.

She looked at Gao, and for the first time, she saw the shadow under his eyes. He was tired. Not the tiredness of a long walk, but the tiredness of a man who is carrying a secret that is too heavy to set down.
pages.image: A young girl with clay on her cheek standing behind a wooden counter, looking defiant, Shen Yu in a brown vest tapping a staff on flagstones, Master Gao in a green robe looking away, Wen in a pale tunic watching the girl, dusty street light.

pages.text:
Auntie Mo had not been in Shitou when the caravan arrived, but she was there now, standing in the shadow of a narrow alley with her bamboo pole leaning against the wall. She had followed them, silent as a reed in a still pond, and her face held the map of the last three days of walking.

"The trackers talk," she said, her voice low and rough. "They do not talk about the water. They talk about the pools."

Wen stepped closer, her heart beating a steady, worried rhythm against her ribs. "Pools?"

"Great round stone pools," Mo said. "In the hills. They are sealed with the same round gate you saw on the jars. The trackers say the pools are filled every night. They say the water is cold, and it is clear, and it does not smell of the river."

Shen Yu’s face went white. "That is not possible," he said. "The river is dry. Where is the water coming from?"

Mo looked at him, and her eyes were hard. "That is what you need to find out, boy. Not where it is going. Where it is coming from. The trackers say the pools are deep. Deeper than the river. And they say the water is taken by men who do not eat, do not sleep, and do not speak."

Wen felt a surge of anger, hot and bright, that surprised her. It was not the anger of a girl whose water had been stolen. It was the anger of a girl who had been told that the world was fair, that the river belonged to everyone, and then shown a ledger that said otherwise.

She looked at Gao. He was standing a few paces away, his arms crossed, his face unreadable. She wanted to ask him, to demand the truth, but the words stuck in her throat. Because if he was innocent, she would have accused him of a crime he did not commit. And if he was guilty, she would have given him the warning he needed.

Mo came closer, and her voice dropped to a whisper. "I will follow the track," she said. "I know the hills. I know the water. I will see what is in those pools."

Wen looked at her, and for the first time since the river stopped, she felt a small, fragile hope. Not a solution. Not an answer. Just a direction.
pages.image: Auntie Mo, short and wide with a conical bamboo hat and a bamboo pole, standing in a narrow alley shadow, speaking to Wen in a pale tunic and Shen Yu in a brown vest, dusty light, tense atmosphere, Wen’s blue ponytail visible.

pages.text:
The caravan pitched its tents on a flat ledge above the town. Stars hung low and sharp, like nails driven into the dark sky, while the air carried the scent of heated stone and distant embers. Wen sat beside the fire, knees drawn to her chest, watching the flames lick at the dry wood.

Gao sat across from her, his face half-swallowed by shadow. He drank from a small clay cup, the water inside clear and still. He did not offer her a cup. He did not offer Shen Yu one, either. The sound of liquid touching his lips was the loudest thing in the silence.

"Tomorrow," Gao said, his voice smooth as oiled silk, "we take the upper road. It is longer, but safer. The lower path is crowded with merchants. We do not want to be seen."

Wen watched him. The firelight caught the sharp edges of his eyes. "The lower road," she said. "It is shorter. And it cuts through the hills where the pools are."

Gao’s smile did not waver, but his fingers tightened around the rim of the cup. "The lower road is dangerous. Bandits. Landslides. It is not safe for a girl traveling alone."

"I am not traveling alone," Wen replied. "I have a guide. I have a surveyor. I have a ferrywoman who knows these hills better than anyone."

Gao looked at her, and for a moment, his mask slipped. A flicker of frustration crossed his face, not fear, but the irritation of a man trying to hold a door shut against a rising wind.

"I will not change the road," he said. "But I will watch your back. That is what a guide does."

Wen glanced at Shen Yu. He sat by the fire, his face pale and serious, his glasses reflecting the orange glow. She looked at Mo, who stood at the edge of the camp, her silhouette sharp against the starry sky. Then she looked back at Gao. The cold knot in her chest tightened.

She wanted to trust him. She wanted to believe he was trying to help. But the round seal on the jar was still burning in her mind, and the memory of the wet track in the dust was etched into her bones.

She lay awake, listening to the fire crackle, and wondered if she was wrong to doubt a friend, or right to doubt a stranger.
